newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mostly off in US, pace of rise questioned.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mostly off in US, pace of rise questioned.

text.p: The dollar retreated against the mark and ended little changed versus the Japanese yen on Thursday, as market participants took a deep breath and reassessed the rapid pace of the U.S. currency's recent ascent.

Remarks from Japanese finance official Eisuke Sakakibara rekindled worries that Japan may intervene to defend the ailing yen, and jitters ahead of an upcoming summit meeting of the Group of Seven industrial nations also contributed to the dollar's lackluster performance.
But dealers said the dollar remains firmly supported by a solid U.S. economic backdrop and that Wednesday's retreat was probably little more than a pause before additional dollar gains.

"The market has been forced to reassess the speed with which the dollar will continue to correct upwards," said Hillel Waxman, first vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York. "Trading has become somewhat lackluster, but all the fundamentals are still in place for the dollar to go higher."
The dollar ended the day at 121.80/85 yen, little changed from 121.80/90 at the open. Against the mark, the dollar settled at 1.6360/65, below its opening rate of 1.6410/15.

Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, known as "Mr. Yen" for his influence on the currency markets, told a Japanese news agency on Thursday that his government would intervene to defend the yen at the proper time if the weak currency was harming the Japanese economy.
The remarks knocked the dollar down below 122 yen and sparked worries that G7 nations could call for an end to the dollar's sharp climb when they meet in Berlin on February 8.

But the damage was fairly well contained in Asian trade and the dollar remained steady throughout the U.S. session. Dealers attributed the dollar's fortitude to the stubborn U.S. defense of its strong dollar policy.
On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated that U.S. policy on the dollar was unchanged.

"You never know if independent nations will take some action at some point to slow the dollar's rise," said Seth Garrett, chief foreign exchange dealer at Credit Suisse First Boston, said referring to Sakakibara's remarks.
"But Rubin keeps reiterating that U.S. strong dollar policy is unchanged and that is underpinning it somewhat," he added.
The dollar traded in an extremely tight range against the mark and the yen for much of U.S. trade on Wednesday, finding strong support above the 121 yen and 1.63 mark levels.
Remarks from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, who testified before the Senate Finance Committee on Thursday, sparked little reaction in the currency markets.
But uncertainty ahead of key fourth quarter U.S. growth figures, due Friday, and next week's Fed policy meeting, had traders hesitant to push the dollar higher.
In other trade on Thursday, sterling retreated to end lower at $1.6135/45 against $1.6202/12 at the open, after a fleeting rise on stronger-than-expected U.K. consumer credit figures.
